title: Physicists Find Evidence of a One-in-10-Billion Particle Decay
summary:
Imagine searching for something for more than 40 years. Now imagine it happens only once in every 10 billion tries. That is what physicists at CERN have just found evidence of: an extremely rare particle decay.

The decay is called 'Bd to mu mu.' In it, a particle containing a beauty quark turns into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons. Beauty quarks are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of ordinary matter. They live for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Researchers at the University of Manchester played important roles in the international effort. The result has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma, which counts as evidence but not yet a confirmed discovery. Physicists usually wait for five sigma before announcing a discovery.

So why chase something so rare? Because rare decays are sensitive tests. The Standard Model, the leading framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact, predicts how often this decay should happen. If the measured rate differs from the prediction, even slightly, it could hint at unknown particles or forces. Studying these decays may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider.

Professor Chris Parkes, head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration while its major upgrade was built. He compared the odds to finding one perfect match among everyone on Earth on the very first try.

Detecting the decay took extraordinary instruments. One key part is the Vertex Locator, a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from UK researchers. It tracks the paths of particles made in collisions inside the collider.
why_it_matters: If the measured rate differs from the Standard Model prediction, it could point to unknown particles or forces, so this rare decay may help physicists understand the basic building blocks of matter.

background_read: CERN runs the Large Hadron Collider, a huge machine that smashes tiny particles together at very high speeds so scientists can study what they are made of.
The LHCb experiment is one of the detectors at the collider, built to study particles that contain beauty quarks.
The Standard Model is the leading framework that describes fundamental particles and how they interact, and it predicts how often rare decays should happen.
Physicists compare new measurements with those predictions, because a difference could point to unknown particles or forces.
